analysis.one_liner: Taxes 95% of large corporations' profits above their pre-2015-2019 average, through 2024.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in April 2022 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a temporary windfall-profits tax on large corporations—those with average annual gross receipts of at least $500 million—taxing 95% of profits above an inflation-adjusted average of the company's profits from 2015 through 2019, capped at 75% of the company's taxable income. It was aimed at companies posting record profits during the 2021-2022 inflation surge. The tax would run only through 2024, and the bill does not earmark the revenue for any specific purpose. It was introduced by one House Democrat with four Democratic cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The revenue would go to the U.S. Treasury, reducing the deficit or funding general programs rather than flowing to a named beneficiary. Indirectly, households strained by 2021-2022 inflation would benefit if the tax slowed corporate price increases or shifted the cost of deficit reduction onto profitable corporations.

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes 95% of the 'excess profits' of corporations with at least $500 million in average annual gross receipts—profits above the company's inflation-adjusted average for 2015-2019—so companies doing unusually well during the inflation surge would pay much more on those gains.
The tax is capped at 75% of a company's modified taxable income, and it excludes smaller businesses entirely by applying only to corporations above the $500 million gross-receipts threshold.

The bill tightens several tax bases before measuring profits: it counts profits parked in foreign subsidiaries (by zeroing the 'tangible income' return under GILTI and disallowing the FDII/GILTI deduction), uses slower depreciation, and limits the deductible pay of executives and high earners by extending the $1 million executive-pay deduction cap beyond the five top officers to any individual performing services for the company.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations—particularly those with outsized profits relative to 2015-2019, such as oil producers, shipping lines, and large retailers—would bear the tax. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices, and some could come out of shareholder returns or planned investment. Small businesses under the $500 million threshold pay nothing.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not direct the revenue to any consumer benefit, so households facing high prices would not see money returned to them; the proceeds would simply go to the general Treasury.

Taxing profits above a fixed 2015-2019 baseline at 95% could discourage companies from expanding output in shortage periods, since the marginal profit on added production would be mostly taxed away—an objection economists raised to similar windfall-profit proposals during the 2022 price surge.

The bill carves out regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and S corporations, meaning some of the largest real-estate and investment structures would escape the tax entirely while operating companies pay it.

Economists have long debated windfall-profits taxes: they can raise substantial revenue from past gains but create uncertainty for future investment decisions, and the 2015-2019 baseline does not account for businesses that were small or new before 2015.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, measurable group—very large companies earning far above their pre-inflation average—without touching small business, and its cap limits the risk of confiscatory taxation. But it is a blunt instrument: the revenue is not tied to any relief for households, the carve-outs for real estate and investment companies are hard to defend, and a 95% rate above a fixed baseline risks discouraging the extra production that would actually bring prices down. As a deficit-reducer and a signal about corporate pricing power it has real value; as consumer relief it is indirect at best.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamaal Bowman introduced the bill on April 7, 2022, with Reps. Tlaib, Newman, Schakowsky, and Jayapal as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, which was the only action the bill ever received.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large corporations that would have paid the tax—the oil, shipping, retail, and other big companies posting record profits during the inflation surge—avoided it entirely, because the Ways and Means Committee never considered the bill and no chamber ever voted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations that escaped the windfall tax

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax 95% of large corporations' profits above their 2015-2019 average.

for.name: Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Marie Newman, Jan Schakowsky, and Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup, hearing, or vote; it remained unreferred-action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats, four of them members of the progressive wing; no Republican cosponsored the bill and the Democratic committee chair declined to move it.

industries.industry: Large corporations with windfall profits (oil and gas, shipping, large retail chains)
industries.note: These companies would have paid 95% of profits above their inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, plus tightened rules on foreign profits and executive pay deductions. Their interest in killing the bill ran against households who would benefit from the revenue and potentially slower price increases.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts and regulated investment companies
industries.note: The bill expressly exempts REITs and RICs, so these structures would have avoided the excess-profits tax that operating corporations of the same size paid.
Businesses below the $500 million gross-receipts threshold are entirely outside the tax, so they face no new burden.
